title: Flat Base Breakout
teaches: The flat base breakout as we trade it: a leader rests in a box near its highs above the 50-day and 200-day, the pivot is the base's highest high, the buy is the trade through it at market in regular hours, the stop sits a few cents under the breakout day's low, a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: One, two or three weeks do not get the job done.
facts.claim: IBD: one, two or three weeks do not make a base.

facts.quote: The stock's price declines no more than 15% from its intraday peak to intraday trough.
facts.claim: IBD: a flat base declines no more than 15% from its intraday peak to its intraday trough.

facts.quote: The correction within a flat base should be no more than 15% from its intraday high to the bottom of the pattern.
facts.claim: IBD: the correction inside a flat base is no more than 15%.

facts.quote: It should look like a rectangular box with a correction from high to low of no more than 15%.
facts.claim: IBD: a flat base looks like a rectangular box.

facts.quote: the "flat" base has kind of a "U" shape and doesn't look so flat.
facts.claim: IBD allows a flat base with a slight U shape.

facts.quote: Flat bases should show tight trading.
facts.claim: IBD: flat bases should show tight trading.

facts.quote: These shallow patterns often start forming as a stock takes a breather after an earlier advance.
facts.claim: IBD: a flat base forms as a stock rests after an earlier advance.

facts.quote: In a weekly chart, look for periods of sideways movement or mild declines following a prior uptrend of at least 30% in price.
facts.claim: IBD: look for sideways movement after a prior uptrend of at least 30% (stated for any base).

facts.quote: The typical buy point is the price high made before the decline, plus 10 cents.
facts.claim: IBD's buy point is the high before the decline plus 10 cents.

facts.quote: To get the proper buy point, add 10 cents to the highest price in the pattern, which is usually the start of the base.
facts.claim: IBD's buy point is 10 cents above the highest price in the pattern, usually the start of the base.

facts.quote: The buy point in a flat base is 10 cents above the left-side high.
facts.claim: IBD: the flat base buy point is 10 cents above the left-side high.

facts.quote: Sometimes you can draw a trend line connecting at least three points along the top of the base and find the lowest potential entry.
facts.claim: IBD draws a line across at least three points along the top of the base.

facts.quote: you want to see volume bulge at least 40%-50% above average when a stock breaks out of the flat base.
facts.claim: IBD wants breakout volume at least 40% to 50% above average.

facts.quote: A breakout needs to produce a gain of at least 20% in order to be counted as one stage.
facts.claim: IBD: a breakout counts as a stage only if it gained at least 20%.

facts.quote: Breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up.
facts.claim: IBD: breakouts from late-stage bases often blow up.

facts.quote: It's usually best to buy when a stock breaks out from a first-stage or second-stage base.
facts.claim: IBD: it is usually best to buy a first-stage or second-stage base.

facts.quote: One guideline is the 7%-8% sell rule.
facts.claim: IBD's general loss limit is the 7% to 8% sell rule.

facts.quote: Flat bases form over a 5 to 65 week range. The minimum depth is 0% with a maximum of 15%.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: a flat base is 5 to 65 weeks long and 0% to 15% deep.

facts.quote: Flat bases often occur after a stock runs up after breaking out of one of the other chart patterns.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: flat bases often follow a run-up out of another pattern.

facts.quote: In the case of a Cup, Flat Base, Consolidation or IPO Base, the Pivot corresponds to the Left Side High that began the base.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: a flat base's pivot is the left-side high that began the base.

facts.quote: In most cases, it is the highest intra-day price over the last 100 days (or 20 weeks)
facts.claim: MarketSmith: the left-side high is usually the highest intraday price of the last 100 days.

facts.quote: The percent decline from the start of the base (left side high) to the bottom (intraday low) of the base.
facts.claim: MarketSmith measures depth from the left-side high to the base's intraday low.

facts.quote: Stocks emerging from third, fourth or later stage bases are late in their moves and may be more likely to fail.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: third, fourth or later stage bases are late and more likely to fail.

facts.quote: The Base Stage and Count are always reset to 1 once an intraday low price undercuts the low of the previous base.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: the base count resets to 1 when price undercuts the prior base's low.

facts.quote: The Pivot Range is 0% to 5% above the pivot point
facts.claim: MarketSmith's buy range is 0% to 5% above the pivot.

facts.quote: A prior uptrend of 30% or more: This is the initial strong move that leads into the consolidation phase.
facts.claim: TraderLion: a prior uptrend of 30% or more leads into the base.

facts.quote: the stock's price should not fall more than 15% from its highest point within the base.
facts.claim: TraderLion: no more than 15% off the base's high.

facts.quote: the trading volume should be at least 40% higher than its average volume (1.4 times the relative volume).
facts.claim: TraderLion: breakout volume at least 40% above average.

facts.quote: A well-formed flat base should have tight and orderly price action
facts.claim: TraderLion: a well-formed flat base is tight and orderly.

facts.quote: Flat base breakouts are more likely to succeed in a strong, bullish market.
facts.claim: TraderLion: flat base breakouts do better in a strong, bullish market.

facts.quote: In almost all cases, one-, two-, and three-week bases are risky. They should be avoided.
facts.claim: TraderLion, quoting O'Neil: one-, two- and three-week bases are risky.

facts.quote: Wide and loose bases are a big sign of real danger.
facts.claim: TraderLion: wide and loose bases are a sign of danger.

facts.quote: This is nothing but Darvas box setup.
facts.claim: Bonde: the flat base is a Darvas box.

facts.quote: A big move higher sometime in the past 1-3 months. This move can be anywhere from 30-100%+ and usually lasts a few days to a few weeks.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: a big move of 30% to 100% or more in the past 1 to 3 months comes first.

facts.quote: During the consolidation the stock price "surfs" the rising 10- and 20-day. and sometimes toe 50-day moving average.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: in the consolidation price surfs the rising 10- and 20-day and sometimes toes the 50-day.

facts.quote: Stop is always lows of the day and stop should not be wider than the ATR or ADR of the stock
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day and no wider than the stock's ATR or ADR.

facts.quote: This method can also be traded by anticipating the breakout but I don't find it as effective
facts.claim: Kullamagi finds anticipating the breakout less effective.

facts.quote: If a beginner stick to the 10-day. You wait for the first CLOSE below the 10- day.
facts.claim: Kullamagi trails on the 10-day and sells on the first close below it.

facts.quote: Price should touch one trendline at least three times and twice on the other trendline, using distinct peaks and valleys
facts.claim: Bulkowski's rectangle touches one line at least three times and the other twice.

facts.quote: Trends downward 70% of the time.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: volume inside a rectangle top trends down 70% of the time.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first, a few cents under the day's low; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The first trim: the hard rule is a third at 3R; ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R, and in practice he mostly waits for 5R.
facts.claim: B19: breakeven between 2R and 5R; the hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average.
facts.claim: C29: skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.

facts.quote: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups, except parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
facts.claim: C31: buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: Prefer stocks with growing sales and earnings; the chart comes first.
facts.claim: D40: growing sales and earnings preferred; the chart comes first.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: D41: a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: After the first third at 3R: another third at 5R, then trail the last third; adjustable.
facts.claim: E51: another third at 5R, then trail the last third.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 10-day average for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.
facts.claim: E52: trail the 10-day for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: F63: a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a market correction, when the reading turns Green again, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work
facts.claim: F68: after a correction, start with a few positions and add as they work.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: The same stock: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
facts.claim: E56: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock.

facts.quote: The pivot is the highest intraday high of the base. IBD adds 10 cents; with market orders the 10 cents does not matter.
facts.claim: The pivot is the base's highest intraday high; IBD's 10 cents does not matter with a market order.

facts.quote: Price trades above the pivot during regular hours. Buy with a market order. Set the alert at the pivot.
facts.claim: The trigger: price trades above the pivot in regular hours; buy at market; alert at the pivot.

facts.quote: The ceiling: two or more separate touches of the top within 0.5 ATR, the first at least 10 sessions back.
facts.claim: The ceiling needs two or more separate touches, the first at least 10 sessions back.

facts.claim: On the breakout day price is above the 50-day and the 200-day, with the 50 above the 200.

facts.quote: A few cents under the breakout day's low.
facts.claim: The stop: a few cents under the breakout day's low.

facts.claim: An undercut of the base low ends the flat base; a reclaim within 3 sessions is a U&R.

facts.quote: Before the trigger: a close under the 200-day.

walkthroughs.title: NUS, September 2013: the textbook shelf
steps: NUS, September 2013. The stock nearly doubled, then shelves six weeks, riding the rising 10 and 21-day. Three taps of 90.
Context and pattern check out: above its 50-day and 200-day, shallow at 10.3%, tight, a flat ceiling. The pivot is 90.
2013-09-09: it trades through 90 on 1.9x volume. Buy at market, 90.01. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 88.22.
Failure mode: a close back inside the base, stop taken next day. Instead it reaches 3R the next session. Trim a third.

walkthroughs.title: ALLY, June 2019: tight at the end
steps: ALLY, 2019. A leader rests 11.2 weeks after a 31% run, only 5.5% deep: the shallowest base of the ten.
Four taps of 30, and inside days into the breakout. That is tight at the end, the rule in one picture.
2019-06-27: it clears 30 on 1.80x volume. Buy at market, 30.28. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 29.79.
Failure mode: a close at the low, back in the base. Instead it grinds to 3R on day 10. Slow still pays.

walkthroughs.title: WSM, September 2023: the throwback and the trims
steps: WSM, 2023. An 8-week shelf, 14.6% deep, four taps, after a 30% run. On 2023-09-25 it breaks out on 4.99x volume.
Buy at market, 73.16. Stop under the day's low, 72.24. 3R the next day: a third off, stop to breakeven.
5R by day 10: another third off. Then a throwback to 71.56, through the pivot and the original stop.
Failure mode: a close back inside the base. It came after both trims were due; the trail rode the run to 99.

questions.q: In one line, what is a flat base?
choices: A boxy rest near highs after a run
A V-shaped bottom after a hard crash
A pole that doubles in a few weeks
questions.answer: A boxy rest near highs after a run
questions.why: A boxy rest near the highs after a run. IBD: it should look like a rectangular box, forming as a stock takes a breather after an earlier advance.
questions.lesson_line: A flat base is a leader catching its breath in a box near the highs.

wrong.A V-shaped bottom after a hard crash: That is a bottoming pattern after a drop. A flat base rests near the highs after an advance.
wrong.A pole that doubles in a few weeks: That is the high tight flag's pole. A flat base is the rest, not the run.
wrong.A drift under the falling 200-day: Below the 200-day we do not buy. A flat base sits above its rising averages.

questions.q: On a flat base, where is the pivot, the level a breakout has to trade through?
choices: The midpoint of the base's range
questions.why: The highest intraday high of the base. IBD adds 10 cents to it; with a market order the 10 cents does not matter.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is the top of the box. Mark it before the open.

wrong.The base's lowest intraday low: That is the base low, the floor. The breakout goes through the ceiling.
wrong.The rising 50-day moving average: The 50-day is support inside the base, not the trigger.
wrong.The midpoint of the base's range: Halfway up the box is still inside the box. Nothing has broken out.

questions.q: On a flat base breakout the stop goes a few cents under the base low.
questions.why: False. The stop goes a few cents under the breakout day's low. The base low is not the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the breakout day's low.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On the breakout day price is above the 50-day and the ___-day, and the 50 sits above it.
questions.why: 200. Price above the 50-day and the 200-day, the 50 above the 200. No longs below the 200-day is a hard rule.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 50, above the 200, and the 50 over the 200. Then look at the box.

questions.q: A flat base pivot is 60.00. When do you buy?
choices: At the first daily close above 60.00
In premarket, if it gaps over 60.00
questions.why: As it trades through 60.00, regular hours, bought at market. Set the alert at the pivot and let the trade come to you.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger is the trade through the pivot. Alert at the pivot, market order, regular hours.

wrong.At the first daily close above 60.00: Waiting for the close can cost a day's move. The trigger is the trade through, in regular hours.
wrong.In premarket, if it gaps over 60.00: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
wrong.Inside the base, just under 60.00: That is anticipating with no trigger. Kullamagi finds it less effective; we wait.

questions.q: Volume drying up in the second half of the base is a grade cue, not a gate.
questions.why: True. Drying volume on the right side grades the base up; it is not a gate. Bulkowski's rectangles see volume trend down 70% of the time.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet volume into the right side is a plus, not a must.

questions.q: Our card wants a flat base to be the first or second base since the last stage reset.
questions.why: True. First or second base. IBD: it is usually best to buy a first-stage or second-stage breakout; later bases are late in their moves.
questions.lesson_line: Count the bases. The first two are the ones we want.

questions.q: Growing sales and earnings are preferred, but the chart comes first.
questions.why: True. Prefer stocks with growing sales and earnings; the chart comes first.
questions.lesson_line: Numbers help. The chart decides.

questions.q: Where does a flat base start?
choices: At the lowest low of the base
At the first close over the 50-day
questions.why: At the left-side high, the highest intraday high of the last 100 sessions. Length, depth and the pivot all measure from there.
questions.lesson_line: Find the left-side high first. Everything else is measured from it.

wrong.At the lowest low of the base: The low is the bottom of the box, found later. The base starts at its first high.
wrong.At the first close over the 50-day: The 50-day is a line inside the base, not its start.
wrong.On the breakout day: That is where the base ends, not where it starts.

questions.q: Over the last ten sessions a base spans under half its depth, and the last three include an inside day. Our card's name for that?
questions.why: Tight at the end. IBD: flat bases should show tight trading. Our test: the last 10 sessions inside half the depth, or an inside day in the last 3.
questions.lesson_line: Tight at the end is the tell. Inside days into the pivot are the picture.

wrong.Wide and loose: The opposite. Wide and loose is bars growing, not shrinking.
wrong.A late-stage base: Stage is about how many bases came before, not how tight this one is.
wrong.A climax run: A climax is a vertical burst with gaps and volume, nothing like a quiet inside day.

questions.q: Does the top count as a flat ceiling?
choices: No, the taps are too far apart
questions.why: Yes. Two or more separate touches of the top make the ceiling, the first at least 10 sessions back. Three clean taps is the A+ cue on our card.
questions.lesson_line: A ceiling is touched, not guessed. Two taps make it; three make it clean.

wrong.No, it needs five taps: Two or more separate touches is the rule. Five is a wish.
wrong.No, the taps are too far apart: Spacing is the point: separate swings, the first well back. Far apart is good.

questions.story: A stock rests nine weeks under 48. It tapped 48 three times, each tap a separate swing, the first one six weeks ago. The floor holds near 43.

questions.q: Before the trigger, a close under the 200-day is only a warning. The setup stays alive.
questions.why: False. A close under the 200-day before the trigger invalidates the setup. A brief shakeout under the 50-day is allowed.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, there is no flat base to buy.

questions.q: At the breakout the stock is 12% above its 10-day average. Our rule?
choices: Buy, the pivot is what matters
questions.why: Skip it. A long more than 10% above its 10-day average is too stretched to buy.
questions.lesson_line: A breakout that is already stretched is a chase with a different name.

wrong.Buy, the pivot is what matters: The pivot is the trigger, not the whole rule. The stretch rule still applies at the fill.
wrong.Buy half size: Size does not fix a stretched entry. The rule is skip.
wrong.Wait for the close: The close does not matter here. Distance from the 10-day does.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Never buy a flat base breakout more than ___% above the pivot.
questions.why: 4%. MarketSmith's buy range runs 0% to 5% above the pivot; our line is 4%. Past it, the stop is too far away.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the pivot and I am done. I would rather miss it than chase it.

questions.q: The flat base stop can be a level you watch in your head, as long as you act on it.
questions.why: False. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.

questions.q: A nine-week base: a flat top tapped three times, the same floor each time, one range held throughout. Flat base or VCP?
questions.why: A flat base. It holds one range with a flat top; a VCP's pullbacks shrink one after another. IBD: a rectangular box.
questions.lesson_line: One range, one ceiling, the same floor: that is the box. Shrinking swings are the other setup.

wrong.A VCP: A VCP tightens pullback by pullback. These swings hold one range.
wrong.A cup with handle: A cup is a rounded fall and recovery, then a handle. This is a box.

questions.q: IBD's buy point is the base's high plus 10 cents; our market order at the trade-through makes the 10 cents moot.
questions.why: True. IBD adds 10 cents to the left-side high. We buy at market as price trades through the high, so the 10 cents does not matter.
questions.lesson_line: Same level, no 10 cents. The pivot is the high; the trigger is the trade through it.

questions.q: Buy the breakout today?
choices: Yes, but at half the usual size
Yes, if volume is heavy enough
questions.why: No. No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. If it is still a setup after the report, it can trigger again.
questions.lesson_line: A breakout two days before earnings is a coin flip with a story. Wait.

wrong.Yes, the trigger fired today: The trigger fired, and the calendar still says no. The earnings rule is a hard line.
wrong.Yes, but at half the usual size: Size does not fix a report risk. Smaller is still in.
wrong.Yes, if volume is heavy enough: Volume grades the day. It does not override the earnings rule.

questions.story: The base is clean and tight. The pivot is 112.00 and it trades through this morning. Earnings come after the close in two sessions.

questions.q: Where does the first trim come on a flat base winner, by our hard rule?
questions.why: A third at 3R. That is the hard rule; in practice we mostly wait for 5R. The next third comes at 5R.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, trail the rest.

wrong.Half at 2R: Too early and too much. Breakeven can move at 2R; the trim waits for 3R.
wrong.All of it at 5R: 5R is the second third, not the exit. The last third rides the trail.
wrong.A third at 1R: 1R is where the time stop looks, not where we sell winners.

questions.q: Bought at 90.01 with the stop at 88.22. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 95.38. One R is the fill minus the stop. Add three of those to the fill. NUS reached it the next session.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.

questions.q: We buy flat base breakouts in leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in any group.
questions.why: False. Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups, not any group.
questions.lesson_line: A flat base in a laggard is a box going nowhere. Buy the leaders.

questions.q: The market reading is Orange. Which flat bases may you buy?
questions.why: Only A+ setups. Green is full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts. TraderLion: the setup does better in a strong market.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the box. Orange buys A+ and nothing else.

wrong.Any setup at full size: That is Green. Orange narrows you to A+.
wrong.None, Orange means cash: Red is mostly cash. Orange still allows the best setups.
wrong.Any setup at half size: Orange is about grade, not size. A B setup stays on the bench.

questions.q: What is the trade now?
choices: A flat base breakout at the old pivot
questions.why: A U&R. Once the base low is undercut, the flat base is off. A reclaim within 3 sessions is an undercut-and-reclaim setup, traded as the reclaim.
questions.lesson_line: Lose the floor and the box is gone. The reclaim is its own trade.

wrong.A flat base breakout at the old pivot: The undercut ended the flat base. The old pivot is no longer this setup's trigger.
wrong.Nothing, the stock is broken: A quick reclaim is a shakeout, not a break. It is a different setup, not no setup.
wrong.A short under 71: It reclaimed within two sessions. Shorting a quick reclaim is fighting strength.

questions.story: A nine-week flat base holds a floor at 71. Tuesday the low prints 70.40, under the floor. By Thursday the stock closes back above 71.

questions.q: Tap the words that fit the blank.
questions.sentence: The ___ is not the stop; it can sit a whole base's depth away.
questions.why: The base low. It can be up to 15% away, the base's depth, and the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the breakout day's low, not the bottom of the box.

questions.q: The lowest low before the base was 40.00 and the left-side high is 50.00. The prior advance, in percent?
questions.why: 25%. The left-side high over the lowest low before it, minus one. IBD looks for a prior uptrend of at least 30% before any base; TraderLion and Kullamagi say the same.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the run before the rest. A box with no run in front of it is just a box.

questions.q: Left-side high 100.00, the base's lowest intraday low 86.50. How deep is the base, in percent?
questions.why: 13.5%. The left-side high minus the lowest intraday low, divided by the high. IBD's flat base declines no more than 15% measured that way.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high to low, divided by the high. Measure it; do not eyeball it.

questions.q: Fill 72.20. The breakout day's low is 70.75 and the stop sits five cents under it. How far below the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 2.08%. A few cents under the day's low, and inside the 3% the stop usually sits within. That was APH's stop, 70.70.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.

questions.q: Bought at 30.28, stop 29.79. The stock trades to 32.73. How many R is that?
questions.why: 5R. Each R is the fill minus the stop. That is where the second third comes off; ALLY got there slowly.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. 5R is the second trim.

questions.q: What now?
choices: Hold; the stop is still the exit
Sell at the close, it failed
Widen the stop under the base low
questions.answer: Hold; the stop is still the exit
questions.why: Hold it. A close back inside the base is a warning, not an exit by itself; the stop is the exit. Here the next session's low took the 178.10 stop. A planned loss.
questions.lesson_line: A weak close is a warning. The stop is the decision, and it was made before the open.

wrong.Sell at the close, it failed: We dropped that rule. The stop is the exit; a weak close is a warning.
wrong.Widen the stop under the base low: The stop only moves up, never wider.
wrong.Add, it is cheaper now: Full size at one price with one stop; no adding.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 180.15 with the stop at 178.10. The day closes at 178.15, its low, back inside the base, above your stop.

questions.q: Buy or pass?
choices: Buy half size to cut the risk
Buy, but widen the stop to fit
questions.why: Pass. 94.50 is more than 4% over 90.00. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: I would rather miss it than chase it. Four percent and done.

wrong.Buy, the breakout is confirmed: Confirmed and too far away are both true. The chase line is 4%.
wrong.Buy half size to cut the risk: Half of a bad entry is still a bad entry.
wrong.Buy, but widen the stop to fit: A wider stop to fit a late entry is the mistake, not the fix.

questions.story: The pivot is 90.00. You missed the open. At 10:15 the stock trades 94.50.

questions.q: Where is the stop now?
choices: Get out, the gap is past 2R
questions.why: 50.30. A gap through the stop hands it to the first 30-minute low. That low is inside the 2R ceiling, so it is the new stop.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.Sell at the open, 50.60: The gap rule gives it the first 30 minutes. The open is not the decision; the 30-minute low is.
wrong.No stop until it reclaims 51.00: There is always a stop. The new one is the 30-minute low.
wrong.Get out, the gap is past 2R: The 30-minute low is inside 2R here. The ceiling has not been hit.

questions.story: You bought at 52.00 with the stop at 51.00. It gaps open at 50.60, under your stop. The first 30-minute bar's low is 50.30.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Set the alert at the ___ and buy as price trades through it in regular hours.
questions.why: The pivot. Alert at the pivot, market order as it trades through, regular hours only.
questions.lesson_line: Alert at the pivot. Then the market comes to you.

questions.q: Buy now?
choices: No; wait for a move through 44.00
Yes; buy the inside day at 43.20
Yes; a buy stop in the box at 43.50
questions.answer: No; wait for a move through 44.00
questions.why: No. The trigger is the trade through the pivot in regular hours. Anticipating inside the base with no trigger is a named mistake; Kullamagi finds it less effective.
questions.lesson_line: Feeling it coming is not a trigger. The pivot is.

wrong.Yes; buy the inside day at 43.20: An inside day is the tell that it is tight, not the buy. The buy is the trade through 44.00.
wrong.Yes; a buy stop in the box at 43.50: A stop under the pivot fires inside the base. No trigger has happened at 43.50.

questions.story: The base is tight and the pivot is 44.00. Thursday the stock sits at 43.20, an inside day. You feel it coming.

questions.q: After the entry, a flat base trade that trades down to the stop is sold at the stop, no second thoughts.
questions.why: True. The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider.
questions.lesson_line: My stop is my stop. That is the whole rule.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Hold; the stop stays where it is
Widen the stop to give it room
questions.answer: Hold; the stop stays where it is
questions.why: Hold it. The stop only moves up, never wider. Tests of the pivot are normal: two in three rectangle breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days.
questions.lesson_line: The retest is normal. The stop pays for it; you do not widen it.

wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: Never wider. The rule has one exception and this is not it.
wrong.Sell; the breakout failed: A pullback to the pivot is not a failure. The stop decides, not the retest.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, not on day three at the pivot.

questions.story: Three days after the breakout at 73.16, price slides back to the pivot, 73.00. Your stop is 72.24.

questions.q: When does the stop move to breakeven on a flat base winner?
choices: Never; it stays where it is
At 1R, as soon as it arrives
questions.why: Between 2R and 5R, ideally. The first trim at 3R is the natural moment.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven between 2R and 5R. Earlier is noise; later is giving it back.

wrong.The first higher close: One up day is inside the noise. A normal pullback would hit the stop.
wrong.Never; it stays where it is: The stop only moves up. Moving it up to breakeven is allowed.
wrong.At 1R, as soon as it arrives: Too soon. The card puts breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally.

questions.q: A flat base breakout still under 1R after 10 trading days is held until the stop is hit.
questions.why: False. Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. Every example in our set was past 1R by day ten.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
choices: Sell a third at the open
Move the stop up and hold
questions.answer: Sell a third at the open
questions.why: Sell a third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open. The 3R third comes off right there.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through a trim level is the trim. Take it at the open.

wrong.Wait for the close: The level is already passed. Waiting gives the gap a chance to fill.
wrong.Sell everything: A third at 3R. The rest waits for 5R and the trail.
wrong.Move the stop up and hold: The stop moves up too, but the trim is the rule at the open.

questions.story: Your flat base long sits at 2.6R at Thursday's close. Friday it gaps open to 3.4R.

questions.q: Which is the one thing you never do?
choices: Pull the stop up to 3% to fit the size
questions.answer: Pull the stop up to 3% to fit the size
questions.why: Never pull the stop in to fit. Stop first; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop inside the noise.

wrong.Skip the trade: Skipping is allowed. A3 says so when the honest stop does not fit.
wrong.Wait for a tighter entry: Waiting is fine. The mistake is moving the stop, not the entry.

questions.story: The breakout fills at 48.60. The day's low sits at 46.40, about 4.5% under your fill.

questions.q: This is the stock's fourth base since the stage reset. The shape is clean. Your call?
choices: Pass; it is a late-stage base
A+, a clean and tight shape
B, normal size; the box is clean
questions.answer: Pass; it is a late-stage base
questions.why: Pass. IBD: breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up. Our card wants the first or second base; MarketSmith says later bases are more likely to fail.
questions.lesson_line: A clean box on the fourth floor is still the fourth floor.

wrong.A+, a clean and tight shape: Shape is one row of the grade. Stage is another, and the fourth base fails it.
wrong.B, normal size; the box is clean: A late-stage base is not a size question. It is a pass.

questions.q: What did the stop do?
choices: Its job: a small planned loss
Cost you the trade; it needed room
Nothing; the close was the exit
questions.answer: Its job: a small planned loss
questions.why: Its job. The stop is the exit. Giving it room would have been a 14% hole in three sessions. Stopped out, and that is the cost of being there for the ones that work.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working.

wrong.Cost you the trade; it needed room: Room was a 14% hole in three sessions. The stop saved most of it.
wrong.Nothing; the close was the exit: A mid-range close is not an exit. The stop is.

questions.story: You bought the gap open at 241.28, above the pivot. It closes mid-range on average volume. Next day the low hits your stop at 236.86. Two sessions later it closes 10% under your fill.

questions.q: Which gets the higher grade?
choices: The 1.9x day closing at the high
questions.answer: The 1.9x day closing at the high
questions.why: The 1.9x day closing at the high. IBD wants breakout volume at least 40% to 50% above average, and a close near the high is the A+ row. Both grade the day.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume and a strong close grade the day up. Light volume and a mid-range close grade it down.

wrong.The 0.8x day; quiet is better: Quiet is for inside the base. The breakout wants a crowd.
wrong.Equal; only the pivot matters: The pivot is the trigger. The day's volume and close are the grade.

questions.story: Same base, two breakout days. One trades through on 0.8x its average volume and closes mid-range. The other on 1.9x and closes at the day's high.

questions.q: What is the read?
choices: Wide and loose; the base is off
Still a flat base; the top holds
questions.answer: Wide and loose; the base is off
questions.why: Wide and loose, so the base is off. The last 10 sessions range wider than the first 10. TraderLion: wide and loose bases are a big sign of real danger.
questions.lesson_line: A box that gets louder as it goes is not resting. It is unwinding.

wrong.Still a flat base; the top holds: A flat top over widening bars is a ragged box. The ranges are the tell.
wrong.Tighter is coming; wait: Hope is not a setup. If it tightens again, that is a new base to judge.

questions.story: Six weeks into a base, the daily bars have grown. The last ten sessions swing wider every day than the first ten did. The top is still flat.

questions.q: Does the base still hold the 50-day by our card?
choices: Yes; a brief shakeout is allowed
No; one close under kills it
No; it must never touch the 50-day
questions.answer: Yes; a brief shakeout is allowed
questions.why: Yes. At least 80% of the base's closes at or above the 50-day, and a brief shakeout under it is allowed. Kullamagi: sometimes it toes the 50-day.
questions.lesson_line: Holds the 50-day means most closes, not every close.

wrong.No; one close under kills it: Two days under out of forty is well inside the 80% line.
wrong.No; it must never touch the 50-day: Touching the 50-day is normal in a rest. Living under it is the problem.

questions.story: In an eight-week base the stock closed under its 50-day on two days, a quick shakeout. Then it sat back above it for the rest.

questions.q: Account 50,000. Risk 0.5%. Fill 59.40, stop 57.96. How many shares?
questions.why: 173. Account times risk percent, divided by the fill minus the stop, rounded down. The stop sets the size, never the other way round.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.

questions.q: The last third of a flat base winner trails the 10-day or the 21-day. It is sold on the first touch of the line.
questions.why: False. Sell on a close below the line, not a touch. Kullamagi waits for the first close below the 10-day.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the rising average. Sell the close below it, not the touch.

questions.q: Take the breakout?
choices: No; under $10 and $20 million a day
Yes; the base is the base
questions.answer: No; under $10 and $20 million a day
questions.why: No. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
questions.lesson_line: A clean box in a thin stock is still a thin stock.

wrong.Yes; the base is the base: The base is fine and the stock is not ours. The liquidity rule comes before the chart.
wrong.Yes, half size: Size does not make a thin stock liquid.

questions.story: A clean flat base on a $7 stock that trades about $4 million a day.

questions.q: The stock trades 2,000,000 shares a day on average. Our ceiling on the position?
choices: No ceiling if the stop is tight
questions.why: 20,000 shares. Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume, and not a share more.

wrong.200,000 shares: That is a tenth of the day's volume. You could not get out without moving it.
wrong.No ceiling if the stop is tight: A tight stop cannot catch an overnight gap. The ceiling stands.
wrong.2,000 shares: That is a tenth of the line. The ceiling is 1%.

questions.q: What is it?
questions.why: A cup with handle. A flat base stays boxy within 15% of its high. A rounded fall of 24% with a dip before the buy is a cup. IBD and MarketSmith both cap the flat base at 15%.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the depth. Past the box, it is a cup, with its own rules.

wrong.A flat base: 24% is past every flat base line. The U shape says cup as well.
wrong.A high tight flag: A flag needs a pole that nearly doubles and a short pause. This is a long rounded fall.
wrong.A late-stage base: Stage is about the count of bases, not the shape. The shape here is a cup.

questions.story: The stock ran 60% into a high, then fell 24% over ten weeks in a rounded U. It climbed back near the high. Now it dips a few percent just under the high.

questions.q: What is it?
questions.why: A high tight flag: a pole that nearly doubles, then a pause of a few weeks. A flat base is a longer rest after a smaller run. IBD: one, two or three weeks do not get the job done.
questions.lesson_line: Doubled and paused is a flag. Ran and rested for weeks is a box.

wrong.A flat base: The doubling pole names the setup. A flat base follows a smaller run and rests longer.
wrong.A cup with handle: No rounded fall here. A tight shelf on top of a pole is the flag.

questions.story: The stock doubled in six weeks on news, then paused twelve sessions in a tight range near the top. The pause is 8% deep.

questions.q: Is it a flat base?
choices: No; too deep, a cup-shaped base
Yes; the run before it qualifies
questions.answer: No; too deep, a cup-shaped base
questions.why: No. Past 15% deep it is no longer a flat base; IBD and MarketSmith both stop at 15%. This one was cup-shaped: best 1.1R, stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Three taps do not fix a deep base. Depth is a gate.

wrong.Yes; three taps make it: The ceiling is one gate; depth is another. This fails depth.
wrong.Yes; the run before it qualifies: The run is the context. The pattern still has to be shallow.

questions.story: A 27-session rest after a 51% run, three taps of the top, but the low sits 18.5% under the left-side high.

questions.q: Take it as a flat base?
questions.why: No. Our card wants the close above the 50-day and the 200-day with the 50 above the 200. A base built in a recovery out of a downtrend is not a leader resting. It worked, and it is still not ours.
questions.lesson_line: Price above both lines is half the check. The 50 over the 200 is the other half.

wrong.Yes; price is above both: Price above both with the 50 under the 200 is a recovery, not a leader's rest.
wrong.Yes; the 50 is close enough: Close enough is under. The order of the lines is the rule.

questions.story: A 28-session base after a 42% rebound out of a downtrend. On the breakout day the close is 14% above the 200-day, but the 50-day still sits 1.6% under the 200-day.

questions.q: Closes drifting up 4% of their average from start to end, under a flat top, still count as flat on our card.
questions.why: True. Flat means the line through the closes drifts no more than 10% of the base's average close. A slight U inside that is allowed, as IBD allows.
questions.lesson_line: Flat is a ceiling and a small drift, not a ruler.

questions.q: What was the lesson?
choices: A stop inside the noise gets shaken out
Widen the next stop to the base low
questions.answer: A stop inside the noise gets shaken out
questions.why: A stop inside the stock's normal daily range gets shaken out by noise. You never pull a stop in to fit; and the re-entry on the reclaim is a new trade with its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: A stop that sits inside a normal day is not a stop. It is a coin flip.

wrong.Never buy on heavy volume: Volume was not the problem. The stop's distance was.
wrong.Widen the next stop to the base low: The base low is too far the other way. The honest stop is the day's low, judged against the range.
wrong.Skip breakouts that gap down: The gap came after the buy. The lesson is about where the stop sat.

questions.story: Breakout on heavy volume, but it closes near the day's low. Your stop sits 0.88% under the fill while the stock's average daily range is 2.5%. Next morning a 2% gap down takes the stop; then it reclaims the pivot and runs.

questions.q: Bought at 73.16, stop 72.24. Where is 5R?
questions.why: 77.76. One R is the fill minus the stop; five of those above the fill. WSM got there by day 10, then threw back through the pivot.
questions.lesson_line: Know 5R before the open too. The second third comes off there.

questions.q: What happens to the last third?
choices: Sold on that close under the 21-day
Held; the stop is at breakeven
Sold only if it closes under the base
questions.answer: Sold on that close under the 21-day
questions.why: Sold. The last third trails the 10-day for a fast mover or the 21-day for a steadier one, out on a close below. APH failed back through the base after that; the trims and the trail kept it a win.
questions.lesson_line: Two thirds banked, the last third on the trail. The close below the line is the exit.

wrong.Held; the stop is at breakeven: Breakeven is the floor, not the plan. The trail is the exit for the last third.
wrong.Sold only if it closes under the base: That gives back most of the move. The trail line is closer.
wrong.Added to, on the dip: Full size at one price; no adding. A dip under the trail is an exit, not an add.

questions.story: You bought at 72.20, stop 70.70. It hits 3R on day three and 5R by day ten; you trimmed a third at each. Then it rolls over and closes under the 21-day.

questions.q: Was that loss a mistake?
choices: No; a planned loss on a weak day
Yes; you should have sold at 1.63R
Yes; the stop was too tight
Yes; light volume meant skip it
questions.answer: No; a planned loss on a weak day
questions.why: No. The stop is the exit, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working. By our current default, light volume lowers the grade. It does not cancel a buy made before the day's volume is known.
questions.lesson_line: Light volume lowers the grade, not the rule. A loss at the stop is the plan working.

wrong.Yes; you should have sold at 1.63R: The first trim is a third at 3R. Selling at 1.63R is fear, not a rule.
wrong.Yes; the stop was too tight: A few cents under the day's low is the rule. It held for six days.
wrong.Yes; light volume meant skip it: By our current default, volume is a grading cue, not a gate. And you buy at market before the day's volume is known.

questions.story: A clean six-week shelf, four taps, volume drying up. You buy at market as price trades through the pivot at 206.85, stop 203.95. By the close, volume is only 0.5x and it sits low in its range. It reaches 1.63R, then the stop is hit on day six.

questions.q: By our rules, what came off on the way up?
choices: A third at 3R and a third at 5R
questions.answer: A third at 3R and a third at 5R
questions.why: Two thirds banked. A third at 3R, a third at 5R, stop at breakeven, the last third on the trail. BAC fell back into the base; the trims are what made it a win.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength. The trims are what you keep when the box pulls it back.

wrong.Nothing; it had not reached 10R: Waiting for 10R with nothing banked is how a 5R trade becomes a scratch.
wrong.All of it at 5R: The last third rides the trail. 5R is the second trim, not the exit.

questions.story: Five taps of a 23.5 ceiling after a vertical run. You bought at 23.56, stop 23.12. It reaches 5R in about three weeks, then sinks back into the base.

questions.q: Buy again?
choices: Yes, as a new trade with its own stop
Yes, with a wider stop this time
No; wait for a new base
questions.answer: Yes, as a new trade with its own stop
questions.why: Yes. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. At most 3 tries in a week.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a verdict on the setup. The next trigger is a new trade.

wrong.No; one try per base: The limit is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month, not one.
wrong.Yes, with a wider stop this time: The stop is the day's low again. A wider stop to avoid a repeat is the mistake.
wrong.No; wait for a new base: The base is still there and it triggered again. That is the re-entry.

questions.story: Stopped out of a flat base breakout on Tuesday. Thursday it trades back through the pivot.

questions.q: Bought at 143.20, stop 141.89. You sell a third at 147.13. How many R did that third bank?
questions.why: 3R. The gain divided by the fill minus the stop. LII broke out on light volume and still ran; the stop was tested to the cent first.
questions.lesson_line: Count every exit in R. The first third is 3R.

questions.q: Our flat base stop is IBD's 7% to 8% loss limit, not the breakout day's low.
questions.why: False. IBD's general guideline is the 7%-8% sell rule. Ours is a few cents under the breakout day's low, usually within about 3% of the buy.
questions.lesson_line: Our loss is the day's range, not a percent of the price.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Nothing long; Red is cash and shorts
Buy it; A+ setups trade in any market
questions.answer: Nothing long; Red is cash and shorts
questions.why: Nothing long. Red is mostly cash and shorts. TraderLion: flat base breakouts are more likely to succeed in a strong, bullish market.
questions.lesson_line: The best box in a Red market is a box. Sit on your hands.

wrong.Buy it; A+ setups trade in any market: Orange allows A+. Red allows mostly cash and shorts.
wrong.Buy half size: Half size in a Red market is half a mistake.

questions.story: The reading is Red. A leader shows a textbook flat base and trades through the pivot on heavy volume.

questions.q: How many do you take on day one?
choices: A few; add more as the first ones work
All eight; Green is full risk
questions.answer: A few; add more as the first ones work
questions.why: A few. After a correction, when the reading turns Green again, start with a few positions. Add more only as the first ones work. Many leaders basing sideways is the best setting for the setup.
questions.lesson_line: Green after a correction: a few positions first. Let the winners earn the next ones.

wrong.All eight; Green is full risk: Full risk per grade is the ceiling, not the first day's order. Earn it.
wrong.None; wait a week: Waiting a week after the turn is how you miss the first leg. A few is the rule.

questions.story: After a correction the reading just turned Green. Your list shows eight flat bases sitting at their pivots.

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first trim.
choices: Market at close; stop base low; hold
questions.why: Market at 90.01, stop 88.22, a third at 3R. Market order as it trades through, a few cents under the day's low, the first third at 3R. NUS reached 3R the next session.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, trim, trail. Write it before the open; execute it without a debate.

wrong.Limit 89.50; stop 85.00; out at 2R: A limit under the pivot never fills on the breakout, and a stop down at 85.00 is nowhere near the day's low.
wrong.Market at close; stop base low; hold: The trigger is the trade through, not the close. The base low is not the stop.

questions.story: NUS, September 2013: six weeks flat, three taps of 90, above a rising 50 and 200-day. It trades through 90 on 1.9x volume.

questions.q: Hold through the report?
choices: No; hold through only if up 5R
questions.answer: No; hold through only if up 5R
questions.why: No. We hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. At 2R the gap risk is bigger than the cushion.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings is a gap you cannot stop. Five R buys the ticket; 2R does not.

wrong.Yes; the trend is up: The trend does not report earnings. The gap does.
wrong.Yes; sell half first: Half of a 2R cushion is still under the 5R line.

questions.story: Your flat base long is up 2R and earnings are tomorrow after the close.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before a breakout. Is this base above the 200-day with the 50-day over it? Take it or pass.
choices: Take it; the lines are stacked
questions.answer: Take it; the lines are stacked
questions.why: Take it. Price above the 50-day and the 200-day with the 50 over the 200. A six-week shelf riding the rising 10- and 21-day after the stock nearly doubled. It broke out the next day on 1.9x volume.
questions.lesson_line: Check the lines before the box. Stacked, rising, price on top: that is context.

wrong.Pass; the 50-day is under the 200: Look again: the 50-day runs above the 200-day here.
wrong.Pass; price is under the 200-day: Price sits well above the 200-day, resting on its shorter averages.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before it trades through a flat top. Is the 50-day above the 200-day? Take it or pass.
choices: Take it; price is above the 200-day
Take it; the top is flat
questions.why: Pass. The close was 14.3% above the 200-day but the 50-day sat 1.6% under it. A base built in a recovery out of a downtrend, not a leader resting. It worked, and it is still not ours.
questions.lesson_line: A base that works is not always our base. The lines decide before the box does.

wrong.Take it; price is above the 200-day: Price above the 200 is one line of the check. The 50 under the 200 fails the other.
wrong.Take it; the top is flat: The top is flat and the averages are out of order. Context first, pattern second.

questions.q: IBD counts a breakout as a new stage only when it gained at least 20% before the next base.
questions.why: True. A breakout needs to produce a gain of at least 20% to be counted as one stage. MarketSmith resets the count to 1 when price undercuts the prior base's low.
questions.lesson_line: Count stages by the gains between bases, and start over after an undercut.
